newsitem.title: UK: Landmine ban would deprive UK of four weapon types.
newsitem.headline: Landmine ban would deprive UK of four weapon types.

text.p: Britain's decision to scrap all its anti-personnel landmines by 2005 will deprive the armed forces of four types of weapon including an important anti-runway device dropped by Tornado ground attack aircraft, defence officials said on Wednesday.

The JP233 is not specifically designed to act as an anti-personnel landmine (APL) but since it falls within the strict United Nations definition of what constitutes an APL it will also be scrapped, the officials told reporters.
"The JP233 is something which can't be replaced tomorrow. It is one of the Royal Air Force's major weapons," a defence official said.
The JP233 has two components -- small bombs designed to blow holes in enemy runways and anti-vehicle mines designed to hit bulldozers and tractors sent in to repair the damage.

Foreign Secretary Robin Cook announced the plans to scrap APLs by 2005 in a written statement, but also said the government reserved the right to use the weapons in what he called exceptional circumstances.
"The use of the JP233 would be something ministers would discuss very closely. But it would only be used in major warfare," said one official.

He said if the four kinds of APLs were banned immediately the armed forces could cope by using more costly anti-personnel weapons such as pinpoint artillery fire and airburst bombs designed to explode just above the heads of enemy soldiers.
The other weapons to be scrapped are:
* the Elsie -- or C3 -- APL, which is laid by hand
* the Ranger -- or L10 -- APL, which is fired from vehicles into anti-tank defences to prevent them being dismantled by enemy engineers
* the L-27 anti-tank mine, which although not designed to kill enemy personnel is so sensitive that it can be detonated by the weight of a person
